text:
Help me write an announcement to our staff. I'm the COO of a credit union with 7 branches. We're closing the Maple Street and Route 9 branches on March 31 and moving the people who work there to a new member phone and chat center.

Facts:
- The two branches have 14 staff between them. Every one of them is offered a job in the phone and chat center at the same pay or higher.
- Visits to those two branches fell 44% over the last three years. Phone and chat contacts across the credit union went up 60%.
- Members calling us now wait an average of 9 minutes on hold.
- The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. The branches were open 9 to 5. Shifts will rotate.
- Staff in the center can work from home two days a week after 90 days of training.
- Anyone who doesn't take the new role gets 2 weeks of pay for every year they've worked here.

I want the announcement to say that this change will make everyone's job better. About 400 words, sent by email from me.

Before I draft this, one problem with the main claim and a few questions.

**"This will make everyone's job better" is more than your facts can support.** The good news is real. Everyone keeps their job at the same pay or more. They get two days a week at home after training. And the work goes where members now are: phone and chat contacts are up 60% while visits to these two branches are down 44%, and callers wait 9 minutes on hold. But the 14 people affected are also moving from 9-to-5 to rotating shifts that can run until 8 p.m., and from face-to-face work to phones and chat. Someone with child care at 6 p.m., or who chose branch work because they like seeing members in person, will read "better for everyone" as spin. That makes them less likely to trust the parts that really are good. The severance offer also shows you expect some people won't take the new role.

A version your facts do support: *"Every one of you has a place in this, at the same pay or better. Here's what improves, here's what you'll be asked to do differently, and here's your choice if it isn't right for you."* It names the evening shifts and ends with the choice. I'd recommend that version, but it's your call. If you want to keep the stronger line, I'll write it that way.

Questions, most important first:

1. **Who gets this email, and have the 14 already been told in person?** If this email is how they find out, it needs to be written differently, and I'd advise against doing it that way. If it goes to all staff, people at the other five branches will ask whether they're next.
2. **When do staff have to decide, and when does the center open?** Without a deadline and a start date, people can't plan.
3. **How will the rotation work?** For example, how many evening shifts a month, whether staff can say what they prefer, and whether evening work pays more. This answers the biggest worry.
4. **Where is the center?** The commute is part of whether the job is better. Also, is the 90 days of training paid and on-site?
5. **Severance details:** Is there a minimum or a cap? Does it include benefits, or help finding a new job?
6. **Who can staff talk to, and are meetings planned?** A named person or a date makes the email something people can act on. One more thing: do you know of anything else staff will hear about, like other branches being reviewed or where members of these branches should go next? If so, it's better that it comes from you in this email.

Give me what you have. Anything you don't know yet I'll leave out instead of guessing.

You're right, "better for everyone" goes past what I can show. Use your version.

1. I don't know yet who it goes to or whether the 14 will be told in person first.
2. Written offers go out by February 14, and decisions are due March 1. I don't have the center's opening date.
3. Staff with the most years here pick shifts first. I don't know how many evening shifts a month or whether evenings pay more. I can't promise anyone 9 to 5.
4. The center is at our main office on Elm Avenue. I don't know if the training is paid or on-site.
5. I don't know about a minimum, a cap, benefits, or job help. But anyone who takes the new role and wants out within 6 months can still get the severance.
6. Anyone who wants one can have a one-on-one meeting with HR. I don't know of anything else staff will hear about.

I used your version and left out anything you didn't give me. It's written to all staff and speaks to the 14 directly, so it works for either audience.

<final_document>
**Subject:** Maple Street and Route 9 branches closing March 31: what it means for you

To all staff,

I wanted you to hear this from me. On March 31 we will close our Maple Street and Route 9 branches. The 14 people who work at those two branches will be offered jobs in a new member phone and chat center at our main office on Elm Avenue.

Here is why. Over the last three years, visits to Maple Street and Route 9 fell 44%. Over the same three years, phone and chat contacts across the credit union rose 60%. Today a member who calls us waits an average of 9 minutes on hold. Members have changed how they reach us, and we haven't kept up. The new center puts our people where members are now looking for us.

To the 14 of you at Maple Street and Route 9: every one of you will be offered a job in the center, at your current pay or higher. Here is what the offer gives you and what it asks of you.

- **Hours will change.** The center will be open 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays, and shifts will rotate. I can't promise anyone a 9-to-5 schedule. Shifts will be picked by seniority, so the people who have been here longest choose first.
- **Working from home.** After 90 days of training, you can work from home two days a week.
- **Timing.** Written offers will go out by February 14, and your decision is due March 1.

If the new job isn't right for you, you'll get severance of two weeks' pay for every year you've worked here. If you take the job and decide within six months that it isn't working, you can still leave with that same severance. You don't have to know today whether you'll like it. You can try it.

I know this is a big change. Some of you chose branch work because you like seeing members in person, and evening shifts will be hard for some of you to fit around your lives. I won't pretend otherwise. What I can promise is this: every one of you has a job here if you want it, at the same pay or better, and anyone who tries it and finds it doesn't work has a way out.

If you'd like to talk this through, HR will meet one-on-one with anyone who asks. Please contact HR to set up a time.

Thank you for the care you've given our members at Maple Street and Route 9. That care is exactly what members calling us need.

Chief Operating Officer
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:

- **Signature:** Add your name above the title.
- **Telling the 14 first:** If this goes to all staff, I'd strongly recommend telling the 14 in person before it goes out. If it goes only to them, cut "To the 14 of you at Maple Street and Route 9:" and start that paragraph with "Every one of you."
- **Questions staff will ask that the email doesn't answer:** whether training is paid and on-site, how many evening shifts a month there will be, whether evenings pay more, the center's opening date, and the severance details (any minimum or cap, benefits, job-search help). It would help if HR had answers ready before the one-on-ones start.
- **Members:** Branch staff will also be asked where members of the two closing branches should go. It's worth having an answer ready for them, even though it doesn't need to be in this email.
